pinchSweetPea.title: {{crop}}: pinch out the tips

garlic.about: Grown for its bulbs, each split into cloves. Plant single cloves in autumn or early spring; most types need a spell of cold to split into cloves, so autumn planting gives the biggest bulbs.
garlic.water: Water in dry spells in spring and early summer, while the bulbs swell. Stop once the leaves start to yellow, and water the soil, not the leaves.
garlic.feed: Dig in about two bucketfuls of well-rotted manure or compost per square metre before planting; that is usually all it needs.
garlic.harvest: Lift the bulbs with a fork once the leaves turn yellow: early summer for autumn planting, later for spring planting. Don't wait too long, or the bulbs split and keep badly.
garlic.keeps: Dry the bulbs in a single layer in the sun or an airy shed for two to four weeks, then keep them cool and dry. Hardneck types keep four to six months, softneck types up to a year.

problems.name: Rust
problems.fix: Orange, raised spots on the leaves, worst in damp weather. Give plants room, water the soil rather than the leaves, and clear away the leaves at harvest.

problems.name: White rot
problems.fix: Leaves yellow and wilt, and a fluffy white mould grows on the base of the bulb. There is no cure: lift and bin affected plants, and don't grow garlic, onions or leeks in that bed for many years.

problems.name: Bulbs without cloves
problems.fix: One round bulb instead of cloves, usually from too little winter cold. Plant in autumn next time; the bulb is still good to eat.

garlic.source: Garlic care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State extension. pH: University of Minnesota extension.

broad_beans.about: Grown for the large beans in its pods, the first beans of the year. Sow in autumn or from late winter into spring; tall types need a stake at each corner of the row with string around, and pinching out the tips once the first pods form keeps blackfly away.
broad_beans.water: In the ground, give a good soak when flowering starts and again two weeks later. Pots dry out fast and need water often.
broad_beans.feed: Like all beans, it adds nitrogen to the soil and needs no feed in the ground. In a pot, give a high-potassium liquid feed every two weeks from the first flowers.
broad_beans.harvest: Pick when the pods are full but the beans still small; the scar on each bean should be white or green, not black. Check the lower pods every few days, as they ripen fast.
broad_beans.keeps: Eat shelled beans soon after picking. To keep them, blanch and freeze them.

problems.name: Blackfly
problems.fix: Dense black aphids on the soft shoot tips in late spring. Pinch out the tips once the first pods form, and squash or wash off the rest.

problems.name: Chocolate spot
problems.fix: Dark brown spots on leaves and stems, worst in damp weather and crowded plants. Give plants room, don't add nitrogen feed, and clear away old plants after harvest.

problems.name: Mice
problems.fix: Mice dig up and eat seeds sown outdoors in autumn and winter. Start seeds in pots under cover and plant them out.

broad_beans.source: Broad bean care: RHS. pH: Oregon State University and University of Connecticut extension.

lettuce.about: Grown for its leaves: loose-leaf types are picked a few leaves at a time for weeks, hearting types are cut whole once the heart is firm. It grows fast in cool weather and runs to seed in heat, so sow a short row every two to three weeks rather than all at once.
lettuce.water: Keep the soil moist all the time: a dry spell makes the leaves bitter and the plants bolt. Water in the morning, not the evening, to keep slugs and mould down.
lettuce.feed: In the ground it needs no feeding if compost went in before sowing. In a pot, give a general liquid feed every two weeks in summer.
lettuce.harvest: Pick the outer leaves of loose-leaf types once they are about 10 cm long, or cut the whole plant to a 2.5 cm stump to regrow. Cut hearting types at the base once the heart feels firm; pick in the morning, when the leaves are crisp.
lettuce.keeps: Eat butterhead types soon; crisphead types keep longer in a bag in the fridge.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: Ragged holes and slime trails, worst on seedlings in damp weather. Pick them off at dusk and water in the morning.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: A tall flower stem grows from the centre and the leaves turn bitter, after heat or dry soil. Water regularly, sow summer crops in light shade, and pick before plants get old.

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.fix: Yellow, angular patches on top of the leaves with white fuzz underneath, in cool, damp weather. Space plants for air, water the soil rather than the leaves, and remove affected leaves.

lettuce.source: Lettuce care: RHS. How many to grow: University of Missouri and Kansas State extension. pH: Washington State University extension.

lambs_lettuce.about: A small, hardy salad grown for its rosettes of mild leaves in autumn, winter and early spring, when little else is fresh. It grows slowly and stays low, so keep the bed weeded; the seed does not come up in warm soil, so most sowing is done in late summer and early autumn.
lambs_lettuce.water: Water regularly in dry weather: uneven moisture makes the leaves tough. Outdoors in winter it rarely needs watering.
lambs_lettuce.feed: A light feeder: it grows in any reasonable soil and needs no extra feeding, especially after a well-fed summer crop.
lambs_lettuce.harvest: Cut whole rosettes at the base, or pick a few outer leaves from each plant so new ones grow from the centre. Pick through winter in mild spells; under a cloche or fleece it keeps growing for longer.
lambs_lettuce.keeps: The leaves keep 5 to 7 days in the fridge; wash them just before use.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat the low rosettes, mostly in damp weather. Pick them off at dusk and keep the bed free of weeds, where they hide.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small green or black insects on young leaves, which curl and weaken. Rub them off or wash them away with a strong jet of water.

problems.name: Seeds not coming up
problems.fix: Above about 21 °C the seed stays dormant. Sow again when the weather cools, and keep the soil moist until the seedlings appear.

lambs_lettuce.source: Lamb's lettuce care: RHS and Utah State University extension. pH and keeping: Utah State University extension.

rocket.about: Grown for its peppery leaves, ready four to six weeks after sowing. Salad rocket is an annual that soon flowers, so sow a little every few weeks; wild rocket is a perennial that keeps cropping through summer and autumn.
rocket.water: Keep the soil moist in dry spells: dry soil makes it run to seed early. A pot can need water every day in warm weather.
rocket.feed: It needs no feeding: it grows quickly in most soils and in fresh potting compost.
rocket.harvest: Pick a few leaves from each plant, little and often, which keeps new ones coming. Once the plant flowers the leaves turn tough and hot; the flowers are edible in salads.
rocket.keeps: Best eaten soon; the leaves keep a few days in a bag in the fridge.

problems.name: Flea beetles
problems.fix: Many small round holes in the leaves, worst in warm, dry spells. The damage is mostly cosmetic: keep seedlings watered and cover them with fine insect mesh.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: Flower stems shoot up early in hot, dry weather or when plants are crowded. Thin the seedlings, water well, and sow summer crops in light shade.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat seedlings and young plants. Pick them off at dusk and protect seedlings in damp weather.

rocket.source: Rocket care: RHS. pH: University of Delaware and Oregon State University extension.

spinach.about: Grown for its tender leaves, picked as baby leaves about a month after sowing or as full leaves after about two. It is a cool-season crop that runs to seed in heat and long summer days, so sow it in spring and late summer, and choose a bolt-resistant variety for summer.
spinach.water: It is thirsty: water regularly in dry weather and never let a pot dry out, or it bolts. Water in the morning.
spinach.feed: Dig in compost or well-rotted manure before sowing; on poor soil, rake in a general fertiliser as well.
spinach.harvest: Pick a few outer leaves from each plant every week or so, which keeps new ones coming, or cut the whole crop just above the base to regrow once. Pull out plants that start to flower.
spinach.keeps: Best eaten fresh; it keeps a few days in a bag in the fridge. To freeze, blanch the leaves for 2 minutes, cool them in iced water and pack.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: A flower stalk appears and the leaves turn bitter, after heat, dry soil or long days. Keep the soil moist, grow bolt-resistant varieties, and pull bolted plants.

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.fix: Yellow patches on the leaves with grey-purple fuzz underneath, in cool, humid weather. Thin plants for air, water in the morning, and remove affected leaves.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat the soft young leaves. Pick them off at dusk, water in the morning and keep weeds down.

spinach.source: Spinach care: RHS. How many to grow: University of Missouri and Kansas State extension. pH: Washington State University extension. Freezing: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia).

peas.about: Grown for sweet peas from the pod, or for edible pods (mangetout and sugar snap). Sow from early spring; all but the smallest types climb by tendrils and need netting or twiggy sticks from the start.
peas.water: Water well once the plants start flowering and again two weeks later, so the pods swell. Water the soil, not the leaves; pots need water often.
peas.feed: Peas make their own nitrogen and need no feed in the ground. In a pot, give a high-potassium liquid feed every two weeks from the first flowers.
peas.harvest: Pick shelling peas when the pods are well filled, mangetout and sugar snaps at about 7.5 cm long. Start at the bottom and pick every few days, or the plants stop cropping.
peas.keeps: Peas lose their sweetness fast: eat them the day you pick them, or blanch and freeze them straight away.

problems.name: Pea moth
problems.fix: Small caterpillars inside the pods, often only found when you shell them. Very early and late sowings miss the moth in early summer; fine insect mesh keeps it out.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: A white powder on the leaves, mostly in dry weather in late summer. Keep the soil moist, leave room between rows, and pull out spent plants.

problems.name: Mice and birds
problems.fix: Mice dig up the seeds, and pigeons eat young plants. Start seeds in pots under cover and protect the rows with netting.

peas.source: Pea care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State extension. pH: University of Minnesota extension.

radish.about: Grown for its crisp, peppery roots, ready four to six weeks after sowing. Sow a short row every couple of weeks for a steady supply; spring and late summer sowings do best, as summer heat makes the plants flower and the roots hot. It fits in the gaps between slower vegetables.
radish.water: Keep the soil evenly moist so the roots grow fast and mild: dry soil makes them woody and hot, and a soaking after a dry spell splits them.
radish.feed: Needs no feed: it grows so fast that ordinary garden soil is enough.
radish.harvest: Pull them a few at a time when the roots are about 2.5 cm across. Left in the ground they soon turn woody, bitter and very hot.
radish.keeps: Cut off the leaves and the thin root tip; in a plastic bag in the fridge they keep up to a month.

problems.name: Flea beetle
problems.fix: Tiny round holes in the leaves, mostly in warm, dry weather; usually only cosmetic. Keep seedlings watered and cover them with fine insect mesh.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: Plants send up a flower stalk and the root stops swelling, in hot, dry weather. Sow in spring and late summer, keep watering, and pull bolted plants; their young pods are edible.

problems.name: Split or woody roots
problems.fix: Uneven watering splits the roots; age makes them woody. Water regularly and pick at about 2.5 cm across; split roots are still good to eat.

radish.source: Radish care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: University of Connecticut and University of Maryland extension. Keeping: University of Missouri extension.

carrot.about: Grown for its sweet roots. Sow it thinly where it is to grow, in loose soil without stones: stones, clods and fresh manure make the roots fork. The seedlings are slow and small at first, so keep the row free of weeds.
carrot.water: Carrots cope with dry spells and seldom need water; in a long drought give a good soaking every two weeks. Steady moisture matters more than a lot of it: a heavy watering after a dry spell splits the roots.
carrot.feed: Needs no feed. Do not dig in fresh manure or compost just before sowing, as it makes the roots fork; use ground that was manured for an earlier crop.
carrot.harvest: Pull carrots as soon as they are big enough to use, loosening the soil with a fork first so they do not snap; very large roots lose flavour. When thinning, touch the leaves as little as possible, as their smell draws carrot fly.
carrot.keeps: Cut the leaves to about 1 cm; in a perforated bag in the fridge or a box of moist sand in a cool place they keep 2 to 4 months. Maincrop carrots can also stay in the ground under straw until needed.

problems.name: Carrot fly
problems.fix: Rusty-brown tunnels in the roots, made by small maggots. Cover the whole crop with fine insect mesh from sowing.

problems.name: Forked roots
problems.fix: Roots split into several legs, in stony, lumpy or freshly manured soil. Dig the bed over well and take out stones, or grow short, round varieties.

problems.name: Split roots
problems.fix: Cracks along the root when heavy rain or watering follows a dry spell. In long dry spells water deeply and regularly.

carrot.source: Carrot care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: University of Connecticut and University of Maryland extension. Pot size: University of Illinois extension. Keeping: University of Missouri extension.

parsnip.about: Grown for its long, sweet roots, which stay in the ground from spring into winter and taste sweeter after frost. Buy fresh seed every year: old seed comes up poorly, and even fresh seed takes two to four weeks to appear. The leaves can blister skin in sunshine, so wear gloves and long sleeves when weeding.
parsnip.water: Water young plants in dry spells until they are established; after that the deep roots cope with dry weather. Keep moisture even, as a soaking after a drought splits the roots.
parsnip.feed: Needs no feed. Use ground manured for an earlier crop: fresh manure or compost makes the roots fork.
parsnip.harvest: Lift the roots from autumn, once the leaves die down, ideally after the first hard frost; loosen the soil deeply with a fork first, as the roots are long. Mark the row so you can find it in winter.
parsnip.keeps: Roots keep best in the ground all winter; lift a few extra before hard frost or cover the row with straw. Lifted roots keep 2 to 4 months in a perforated bag in the fridge.

problems.name: Canker
problems.fix: Orange-brown or black rough patches on the top of the root, often where it was damaged. Grow resistant varieties and take care not to injure the roots when hoeing.

problems.name: Carrot fly
problems.fix: Rusty-brown tunnels in the roots, made by small maggots. Cover the crop with fine insect mesh and do not sow where carrots or parsnips grew recently.

problems.name: Poor germination
problems.fix: Gaps in the row, from old seed or cold, wet soil. Use fresh seed, wait for the soil to warm, and sow a few seeds at each spot, keeping the strongest.

parsnip.source: Parsnip care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: University of Connecticut and University of Maryland extension. Keeping: University of Missouri extension.

beetroot.about: Grown for its sweet roots, and its young leaves for salads. Each seed is a cluster that gives several seedlings, so thin them early or let them grow as a small group for baby beets. Sow small amounts every few weeks from spring to midsummer; roots from summer sowings are the ones that store.
beetroot.water: Water seedlings in dry spells; established plants need water only every 10 to 14 days in dry weather. Too little water makes the roots woody, uneven watering splits them, and too much gives leaves instead of roots.
beetroot.feed: Soil improved with compost needs no feed; if plants grow poorly, give a high-nitrogen liquid feed. Keep weeds away, as they take food and water.
beetroot.harvest: Lift every other root once they reach golf-ball size and leave the rest to grow, pulling none bigger than about 7 cm across. Twist the leaves off rather than cutting them, so the roots do not bleed.
beetroot.keeps: Twist off the leaves 2.5 cm above the root; in a perforated bag in the fridge, or in boxes of dry sand in a cool shed, the roots keep 2 to 4 months.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: Plants flower instead of swelling their roots, after hot, dry weather or a very early, cold sowing. Choose bolt-resistant varieties and do not sow too early.

problems.name: Beet leaf miner
problems.fix: Pale brown blotches in the leaves, where small maggots feed inside. Pinch off affected leaves; the roots are rarely harmed.

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.fix: Pale yellow patches on the leaves with grey-purple mould underneath, in damp weather. Remove affected leaves, leave room between plants for air, and water the soil, not the leaves.

beetroot.source: Beetroot care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: University of Connecticut and University of Maryland extension. Keeping: University of Missouri extension.

turnip.about: Grown for its round roots and its young leaves. Early types are ready in about six weeks: sow a little and often in spring, and again in late summer for autumn and winter roots. It needs steady moisture; in dry soil the roots stay small and woody and the plants flower early.
turnip.water: Water in dry weather so the roots grow quickly and stay tender. A pot dries out fast and needs watering often in summer.
turnip.feed: Soil improved with compost or well-rotted manure, ideally the autumn before, is enough; it needs no extra feed.
turnip.harvest: Pull early turnips at golf-ball size to eat raw, or tennis-ball size to cook; bigger roots turn woody and bitter. Young leaves up to 15 cm long can be cooked like spinach.
turnip.keeps: Twist off the leaves; autumn roots keep several weeks in trays of moist sand in a cool, frost-free place. In mild areas they can stay in the ground under fleece.

problems.name: Cabbage root fly
problems.fix: Young plants wilt and small white maggots tunnel into the roots. Cover the crop with fine insect mesh from sowing.

problems.name: Clubroot
problems.fix: Swollen, misshapen roots and plants that wilt on warm days. Lime acid soil and do not grow turnips or other cabbages where it has appeared; it stays in the soil for many years.

problems.name: Slugs
problems.fix: Seedlings eaten overnight, with slime trails. Protect young plants, especially in damp weather.

turnip.source: Turnip care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: University of Connecticut and University of Maryland extension.

chard.about: Grown for its large leaves and thick stalks in white, red or yellow, picked from summer until the cold stops it and again in spring. One sowing crops for months and it bolts less readily than spinach, which makes it one of the easiest leaf crops.
chard.water: Water young plants regularly until they are settled; after that it copes with short dry spells, but water it in long ones. In a pot, water whenever the compost begins to dry.
chard.feed: It usually needs no feeding: it grows well in most soils and in fresh potting compost.
chard.harvest: Cut the outer leaves with their stalks at the base and leave the centre to keep growing. Small young leaves can go raw in salads; cook bigger ones like spinach, giving the stalks a little longer.
chard.keeps: The leaves keep a few days in the fridge. To freeze, blanch them for 2 minutes, cool them in iced water and pack.

problems.name: Leaf miner
problems.fix: Pale brown blotches where small larvae tunnel inside the leaf. Pick off and bin the affected leaves; fine insect mesh keeps the fly off.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They make holes in young plants, mostly in damp weather. Pick them off at dusk and protect the seedlings.

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.fix: Pale patches with grey fuzz underneath on crowded plants in damp weather. Space plants well and remove affected leaves.

chard.source: Chard care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: Washington State University extension. Freezing: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia).

chicory.about: A family of bitter salad leaves: radicchio forms a tight red head, sugarloaf a tall green heart, and endive and escarole a loose rosette that is blanched to make it milder. Sown in early summer they crop from late summer into autumn; sown outdoors too early in spring, they tend to run to seed.
chicory.water: Water thoroughly in dry weather: dry soil makes the leaves more bitter and the plants bolt. Keep the bed weeded so nothing competes for water.
chicory.feed: It usually needs no feeding in the ground. In a pot or on light soil, give a general liquid feed every two weeks in summer.
chicory.harvest: Cut radicchio and sugarloaf heads at the base once they are firm; the stump often sprouts a second, smaller head. Blanch endive by covering the dry heart with a plate or a bucket for about two weeks, then cut it and use it soon.
chicory.keeps: Heads keep several days in the fridge. Keep blanched hearts in the dark: light turns them green and bitter again.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: Flower stems shoot up after cold spells when the plants are young, or in hot, dry weather. Do not sow outdoors too early, water in dry spells, and use bolt-resistant varieties for early sowings.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat seedlings and hide under blanching covers. Look under the covers every few days and remove them.

problems.name: Rot while blanching
problems.fix: The inner leaves rot when the heart is wet under the cover. Cover only dry plants, blanch a few at a time, and check them often.

chicory.source: Radicchio and endive care: RHS. How many to grow: University of Missouri extension. pH: University of Arkansas extension.

kale.about: Grown for its leaves, picked from autumn right through winter, when frost makes them sweeter. It is the hardiest and least fussy of the cabbage family; keep caterpillars and pigeons off it and each plant gives many pickings.
kale.water: Water young plants regularly so the soil never dries out. Once established, water only in long dry spells; a pot needs regular water in summer.
kale.feed: Plant into ground enriched with compost. It needs a feed only on poor soil or in a pot: a nitrogen-rich fertiliser gives it a boost.
kale.harvest: Pick two or three lower leaves from each plant at a time, working up the stem, and leave the top to grow. Regular picking keeps new leaves coming until spring.
kale.keeps: Leaves keep a few days in the fridge, but the plants stand in the garden all winter, so pick as you need. To freeze, blanch for 2 minutes and cool in iced water.

problems.name: Cabbage caterpillars
problems.fix: Holes in the leaves and green caterpillars, from early summer to autumn. Cover plants with fine insect mesh from planting, and rub off clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves.

problems.name: Mealy cabbage aphid
problems.fix: Grey, waxy clusters of aphids on young leaves, which curl and spoil. Squash or wash off small colonies early, and remove badly affected leaves.

problems.name: Pigeons
problems.fix: They tear the leaves in winter, leaving only stalks and veins. Cover plants with netting held clear of the leaves on hoops or canes.

kale.source: Kale care: RHS. How many to grow: University of Missouri and Kansas State extension. pH: Washington State University extension. Freezing: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia).

cabbage.about: Grown for its firm heads; with spring, summer, autumn and winter varieties you can cut cabbage most of the year. It wants firm, fertile ground and protection from caterpillars, pigeons and root fly; do not grow it where cabbage-family crops grew in the last two years.
cabbage.water: Water young plants regularly; once established, give a thorough soak about every 10 days in dry spells, and more once the heads begin to form. A mulch of compost keeps the soil moist.
cabbage.feed: A hungry crop: dig in compost the autumn before. On poor soil, give a nitrogen-rich fertiliser once the plants are settled and before the hearts form.
cabbage.harvest: Cut the head just above the ground with a sharp knife once it is firm. On spring and summer cabbages, cut a shallow cross in the stump: it often grows a second, smaller head.
cabbage.keeps: A head keeps at least a week in the fridge. Winter cabbages keep for months in a cool, dry, frost-free place, or can stand in the ground until needed.

problems.name: Cabbage caterpillars
problems.fix: Holes in the leaves and green caterpillars, from early summer to autumn. Cover plants with fine insect mesh from planting, and rub off clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves.

problems.name: Cabbage root fly
problems.fix: Young plants wilt and die while white maggots eat the roots. Cover new plants with fine insect mesh pinned to the ground, and move the crop each year.

problems.name: Club root
problems.fix: Plants stay small and wilt on warm days; the roots are swollen and knotted. There is no cure and it stays in the soil for years: lime acid soil, rotate crops, raise plants in pots so they go out with strong roots, or grow resistant varieties.

cabbage.source: Cabbage care and keeping: RHS. How many to grow: University of Missouri and Kansas State extension. pH: Washington State University extension.

cauliflower.about: Grown for its white curd, the head that forms in the centre of the plant. It is the fussiest of the cabbage family: any check in growth, from dry soil, loose ground or late planting, gives small, early heads, so keep it growing steadily. In a pot, grow a mini variety.
cauliflower.water: Keep the soil damp at all times but not waterlogged, above all while the heads form. Mulch to hold the moisture; a pot needs water whenever the compost starts to dry.
cauliflower.feed: Dig in compost before planting. On poor soil, feed young plants with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser before the heads form.
cauliflower.harvest: Cut the head with a few leaves once it is firm, before it starts to separate. In summer sun, fold a few leaves over the curd to keep it white, and in winter tie them over it against hard frost.
cauliflower.keeps: Best eaten fresh: it keeps several days in the fridge with a few leaves left on. Florets can be blanched and frozen.

problems.name: Small or button heads
problems.fix: Tiny heads that form early, after a check in growth. Plant young plants on time into firm soil and water steadily.

problems.name: Club root
problems.fix: Plants stay small and wilt on warm days; the roots are swollen and knotted. There is no cure and it stays in the soil for years: lime acid soil to about pH 6.5, rotate crops, and raise plants in pots so they go out with strong roots.

problems.name: Cabbage caterpillars
problems.fix: Holes in the leaves and green caterpillars, from early summer to autumn. Cover plants with fine insect mesh from planting, and rub off clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves.

cauliflower.source: Cauliflower care and keeping: RHS. How many to grow: University of Missouri and Kansas State extension. pH: University of Minnesota extension.

broccoli.about: Grown for its green heads of flower buds: cut the main head and side shoots keep coming for weeks. Pick before the buds open into yellow flowers, which happens fast in warm weather. Sprouting broccoli is a hardier kind that stands over winter and crops in spring.
broccoli.water: Water young plants regularly until they are established, then in dry spells: a check in growth makes it flower early. A mulch of compost keeps the soil moist.
broccoli.feed: A hungry crop: dig in compost or manure before planting. On poor soil, or if growth is slow, give a high-nitrogen feed when the plants are about 20 cm tall.
broccoli.harvest: Cut the main head with some stem while it is firm and the buds are still closed. Then check every few days and cut the side shoots before they flower; regular picking keeps them coming for up to two months.
broccoli.keeps: It keeps a few days in the fridge and freezes well after blanching.

problems.name: Early flowering
problems.fix: Heads stay small and open into yellow flowers, in hot weather or after a check in growth. Water in dry spells, grow bolt-resistant varieties where summers are hot, and cut heads as soon as they are ready.

problems.name: Cabbage caterpillars
problems.fix: Holes in the leaves and green caterpillars, from early summer to autumn. Cover plants with fine insect mesh from planting, and rub off clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves.

problems.name: Pigeons
problems.fix: They tear the leaves, leaving only stalks and veins. Cover plants with netting held clear of the leaves on hoops or canes.

broccoli.source: Broccoli care and keeping: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: Washington State University extension. Pot size: Texas A&M AgriLife extension.

brussels_sprouts.about: Grown for the small buttons that form up the tall stem, picked through autumn and winter; they taste sweetest after frost. It is a long crop that wants firm soil: tread the ground before planting and firm each plant in, or the sprouts grow loose.
brussels_sprouts.water: Water young plants regularly so the soil never dries out; once established, water only in dry weather. A thick mulch keeps the soil moist.
brussels_sprouts.feed: Dig in compost the autumn before. On poor soil, or if growth is slow, give a nitrogen-rich fertiliser in early to mid summer.
brussels_sprouts.harvest: Start with the lowest sprouts once they are firm and about the size of a walnut, snapping them off with a downward tug, and work up the stem. When the sprouts are done, cook the top like spring greens.
brussels_sprouts.keeps: Cut whole stems keep a few days stood in water, or hung in a cool, frost-free shed; pick sprouts as needed. They also freeze after blanching.

problems.name: Loose sprouts
problems.fix: Open, leafy sprouts instead of tight buttons, from loose soil. Firm the soil before planting, earth up the stems in late summer, and stake tall plants in windy places.

problems.name: Mealy cabbage aphid
problems.fix: Grey, waxy aphids on the leaves and inside the sprouts. Squash or wash off small colonies early, and remove badly affected leaves.

problems.name: Club root
problems.fix: Plants stay small and wilt on warm days; the roots are swollen and knotted. There is no cure and it stays in the soil for years: lime acid soil to at least pH 6.5, rotate crops, and raise plants in pots so they go out with strong roots.

brussels_sprouts.source: Brussels sprouts care and keeping: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State extension. pH: University of Georgia extension. Freezing: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia).

kohlrabi.about: Grown for its swollen stem, a crisp ball that sits just above the soil and tastes like a mild, sweet cabbage. It grows fast, so sow a short row every few weeks from spring to late summer rather than all at once. Pick it young: a bulb left to grow big turns woody.
kohlrabi.water: Keep the soil evenly moist: dry spells slow growth and make the bulbs tough. Water young plants regularly until they are well rooted.
kohlrabi.feed: Dig in compost before sowing and mulch once plants are growing. It needs less nitrogen than other cabbages, so no extra feed is needed.
kohlrabi.harvest: Cut the stem below the bulb when it is between golf-ball and tennis-ball size. The young leaves can be cooked like kale.
kohlrabi.keeps: Cut off the leaves and root; in a plastic bag in the fridge it keeps 2 to 4 weeks.

problems.name: Cabbage caterpillars
problems.fix: Green caterpillars eat holes in the leaves. Cover plants with fine insect mesh, or check under the leaves for eggs and caterpillars and pick them off.

problems.name: Flea beetle
problems.fix: Many tiny round holes in young leaves in warm, dry weather. Keep seedlings watered and cover them with fine mesh until they grow away.

problems.name: Woody bulbs
problems.fix: Tough, stringy flesh after hot, dry weather or picking too late. Water in dry spells and pick at tennis-ball size at most.

kohlrabi.source: Kohlrabi care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: University of Connecticut and University of Maryland extension. Keeping: University of Missouri extension.

onion_sets.about: Sets are small onions grown the year before, planted to swell into full bulbs. They are the easiest way to grow onions: push them in with the tip just showing and firm the soil so birds don't pull them out.
onion_sets.water: Water in long dry spells, mainly while the plants are young. Stop once the bulbs have swollen in midsummer: late watering shortens how long they keep.
onion_sets.feed: Compost dug in before planting is usually enough. On poor soil, give sets planted in autumn a nitrogen-rich feed in late winter.
onion_sets.harvest: When the leaves yellow and fall over, lift the bulbs before the leaves die off completely: June to July for autumn sets, July to October for spring ones. Dry them in the sun for about two weeks.
onion_sets.keeps: Keep dry onions in nets or slatted trays somewhere cool, dry, airy and light; in the dark they sprout. Autumn-planted onions keep until early winter, spring-planted ones into the next spring.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: A flower stalk grows from the middle, often after a cold spring. Snap it off and eat that onion first, as it won't keep; heat-treated sets bolt less.

problems.name: White rot
problems.fix: Leaves yellow and wilt, and a fluffy white mould grows on the base of the bulb. There is no cure: lift and bin affected plants, and don't grow onions, garlic or leeks in that bed for many years.

problems.name: Onion fly
problems.fix: Maggots eat the roots and bulb; young plants yellow, wilt and die. Lift and destroy affected plants, and cover the crop with fine insect mesh.

onion_sets.source: Onion care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State extension. pH: University of Connecticut extension.

onion.about: Grown from seed for bulbs that keep through winter; cheaper than sets, with more varieties, and less likely to bolt. Sow in early spring, indoors or in the row, and thin the seedlings in two steps so each bulb has room.
onion.water: Keep seedlings moist; later, water only in long dry spells. Stop once the bulbs have swollen in midsummer, so they keep longer.
onion.feed: Compost dug in before sowing is usually enough; extra nitrogen late on gives soft bulbs that keep badly.
onion.harvest: When the leaves yellow and fall over, from July to October, lift the bulbs before the leaves die off completely. Dry them in the sun for about two weeks.
onion.keeps: Onions from seed keep into the next spring, in nets or slatted trays somewhere cool, dry, airy and light; in the dark they sprout.

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.fix: Pale patches on the leaves with a grey-purple mould, in cool, wet weather; the leaves collapse. Remove affected leaves, give the plants room, and grow onions in another bed next year.

problems.name: Onion fly
problems.fix: Maggots eat the roots and bulb; seedlings yellow, wilt and die. Lift and destroy affected plants, and cover the crop with fine insect mesh.

problems.name: Weeds
problems.fix: Onion seedlings are thin and slow, and weeds soon smother them. Weed by hand often while they are small.

onion.source: Onion care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State extension. pH: University of Connecticut extension.

leek.about: Grown for its long white stems, picked from late summer through winter. Sow in a seedbed or pots, then move the young plants, about pencil thick, into deep holes made with a dibber and fill each hole with water; deep planting gives a long white stem.
leek.water: Water young plants until they are growing well, then in long dry spells. Water at the base and keep the leaves dry, which holds rust back.
leek.feed: Leeks stand in the ground for months and like rich soil: dig in plenty of compost or manure before planting. On poor soil, a nitrogen feed in midsummer helps.
leek.harvest: Lift leeks with a fork as you need them from late summer; taking every other one lets the rest grow bigger. Late types stand through winter, and frost sweetens them.
leek.keeps: Leeks keep best in the ground until you need them. Once lifted, keep them unwashed in the fridge and use them soon.

problems.name: Leek rust
problems.fix: Orange, raised spots on the leaves, worst in late summer. Water at the base and choose a resistant variety if it comes back; lightly affected leeks are fine to eat.

problems.name: Allium leaf miner
problems.fix: Small grubs tunnel into the stems, which twist and rot; lines of tiny white dots on the leaves are the first sign. Cover leeks with fine insect mesh from planting.

problems.name: Leek moth
problems.fix: Caterpillars tunnel in the leaves and leave white, papery patches. Cut off damaged leaves; the same fine mesh keeps the moth out.

leek.source: Leek care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut extension.

celery.about: Grown for its crisp stalks. Self-blanching types are the easiest: plant them in a block, not a row, so they shade each other's stems. Celery needs warmth and steady water: young plants left below 10 °C for long can run to seed, so plant out only once the nights stay mild.
celery.water: Never let the soil dry out: dry spells make the stalks stringy and too strong in flavour. Water generously in summer, in the morning or evening, with rainwater if you can.
celery.feed: Plant into ground rich in compost or manure. On poor soil give a light dressing of high-nitrogen fertiliser in summer; in a pot, a balanced liquid feed every two weeks.
celery.harvest: Lift whole plants from late summer, before the leaves turn yellow and before the first frost; cover them with fleece when nights turn cold. Use them soon after lifting.
celery.keeps: Wrapped in a damp cloth or a bag in the fridge, it stays crisp for a short time; use it soon.

problems.name: Celery leaf miner
problems.fix: Brown, dried-up blotches in the leaves, where small maggots feed inside. Pinch off affected leaves and cover young plants with fine insect mesh.

problems.name: Leaf spot
problems.fix: Small brown spots with tiny black dots that spread over the leaves in wet weather. Remove spotted leaves and do not grow celery or celeriac in the same soil for a few years.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They love celery and eat young plants and stalks. Protect plants, especially in damp weather.

celery.source: Celery care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut and University of Maryland extension.

fennel.about: Florence fennel is grown for its swollen, aniseed-flavoured leaf base, the bulb. Its main problem is bolting, when it runs to flower instead of forming a bulb: sow in early summer rather than spring, choose a bolt-resistant variety, and sow in modules so the roots are not disturbed. Once the base starts to swell, draw soil up around it to keep it white and sweet.
fennel.water: Keep the soil moist all the time: a dry spell is one of the main causes of bolting. Water generously in the morning, and check a pot every day in summer.
fennel.feed: Dig in compost before sowing and mulch once plants are growing; it needs no other feed.
fennel.harvest: Cut the bulb just above the soil when it is 10 to 15 cm across, or from 5 cm for small ones. Do not wait until it lengthens and sends up a stem, as it turns woody.
fennel.keeps: Best eaten fresh; it keeps a few days in a bag in the fridge.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: A flower stem shoots up and the bulb stays flat and tough, after cold, a dry spell or root disturbance. Sow later, keep watering, and use any bolting plant at once.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat seedlings and young plants. Protect plants in damp weather and weed by hand near them, as weeds hide slugs.

fennel.source: Florence fennel care: RHS. pH: Utah State University and University of Arkansas extension.

potato.about: Grown for its tubers. Earlies are dug in early summer; maincrops are dug in autumn and store through the winter. As the shoots grow, draw soil up around them (earthing up): it protects them from frost and keeps the tubers from turning green.
potato.water: Water in dry spells, above all once the plants flower and the tubers are forming; steady moisture then also helps against scab. A pot needs regular watering even in rain, as the leaves keep the rain off the compost.
potato.feed: Grow it in ground improved with compost or manure. On poor soil give a nitrogen-rich fertiliser at the second earthing up; in a pot, mix a general fertiliser in at planting or give a liquid feed after about six weeks.
potato.harvest: Dig earlies when the flowers open, once the tubers are the size of hens' eggs. For maincrops to store, cut off the tops once they yellow, wait 10 days, then dig, starting 30 cm from the stem so you do not spear tubers.
potato.keeps: Dry the tubers for a few hours and brush off the soil. Sound tubers keep 2 to 4 months in paper or hessian sacks somewhere dark, cool and frost-free; check them every few weeks and remove any that rot.

problems.name: Blight
problems.fix: Brown patches that spread fast over the leaves in warm, wet weather, then rot the tubers. Cut off and remove the tops as soon as you see it, wait two to three weeks, then dig; grow resistant varieties.

problems.name: Scab
problems.fix: Rough, corky patches on the skin; the potatoes are still good to eat once peeled. Water in dry spells while tubers form, do not lime before planting, and grow resistant varieties.

problems.name: Green potatoes
problems.fix: Tubers that reach the light turn green and are poisonous. Earth up well, store in the dark, and throw green tubers away.

potato.source: Potato care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: University of Georgia extension. Pot size: Cornell Cooperative Extension. Keeping: University of Missouri extension.

asparagus.about: A perennial grown for its spring spears; a good bed crops for 20 years or more. Plant the crowns in a permanent, weed-free bed and do not cut any spears for the first two years, so the roots can build up strength.
asparagus.water: Water new crowns regularly through their first summer. Established plants root deeply and need water only in long dry spells.
asparagus.feed: Mulch the bed each late winter with 5 cm of compost or well-rotted manure. If growth is weak, scatter a general fertiliser in early spring, before the spears appear.
asparagus.harvest: Cut spears with a sharp knife just below the soil when they are about 18 cm tall, every two or three days in warm weather. Stop after six weeks in the first cropping year and after eight weeks later on; then let the ferns grow, and cut them down only when they turn yellow in autumn.
asparagus.keeps: Spears keep a few days in the fridge, standing in a little water or with the cut ends wrapped in damp paper. Blanched, they freeze well.

problems.name: Asparagus beetle
problems.fix: Red and black beetles with cream spots, and their grey larvae, strip the stems and ferns in summer. Pick them off by hand from late spring and clear old stems in autumn, where the adults spend the winter.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They graze young spears in damp spring weather. Check after dark and remove them, and keep the bed free of weeds and debris where they hide.

problems.name: Root rot
problems.fix: Plants yellow and die back in patches on wet, heavy soil. On heavy ground grow asparagus in a raised bed, and never plant new crowns where asparagus grew before.

asparagus.source: Asparagus care: RHS. How many to grow: University of Missouri and Kansas State extension. pH: Cornell and University of Maryland extension.

rhubarb.about: A long-lived perennial grown for its tart stalks, picked from spring to early summer. Only the stalks are eaten: the leaves contain oxalic acid and must not be eaten. A clump crops for many years; dig it up and divide it every five years or so to keep it vigorous.
rhubarb.water: Water new plants in dry spells through their first season. Established clumps need water only in long dry summers; never let the crown sit in waterlogged soil.
rhubarb.feed: Spread a 7 cm mulch of well-rotted manure or compost around the plant each spring, keeping it off the crown. On poor soil, add a high-nitrogen feed in spring.
rhubarb.harvest: In the second year pull only a few stalks; from the third, pick stalks about 30 cm long. Hold each one at the base and twist it away rather than cutting it, take no more than a third at a time, and stop in early July so the plant can recover.
rhubarb.keeps: Stalks keep about a week in the fridge in a bag; put the leaves on the compost. Chopped, they freeze well.

problems.name: Crown rot
problems.fix: The crown turns soft and brown and the buds die, usually in wet soil in winter. Cut out rotten parts at once; if the whole crown is affected, replant healthy pieces in fresh, well-drained ground.

problems.name: Flower stalks
problems.fix: Tall, thick stems with a large flower head take strength from the plant. Cut them off at the base as soon as you see them.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat the young shoots in spring. Check after dark and remove them.

rhubarb.source: Rhubarb care: RHS. How many to grow: University of Missouri extension. pH: Cornell and University of Maryland extension.

artichoke.about: A large, silver-leaved perennial grown for its flower buds, eaten before they open. It needs space, sun and free-draining soil; cold, wet winters kill it more often than frost alone. In its first summer, cut off the flower stalks so the plant can settle in.
artichoke.water: Water regularly through the first season and while the buds form: dry soil gives fewer, smaller buds. Once established it copes with short dry spells.
artichoke.feed: Dig in plenty of compost before planting and mulch each spring. On poor soil or in a pot, give a high-potassium feed in spring.
artichoke.harvest: Cut buds when they are full size but still tightly closed, with a few centimetres of stem; cut the main bud first and the smaller side buds follow. Check every few days in warm weather, as buds open fast.
artichoke.keeps: Buds keep 3 to 5 days in the fridge in a bag.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Clusters of small black or green insects on the buds and shoot tips. Wash them off with a strong jet of water and leave ladybirds and their larvae to feed on them.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat young plants and new shoots in spring. Protect young plants and remove slugs after dark.

problems.name: Winter losses
problems.fix: Plants rot or die in cold, wet winters, young ones most of all. In late autumn cut the stems down and cover the crown with a thick layer of straw or leaves; uncover it in spring.

artichoke.source: Globe artichoke care: RHS and Utah State extension. pH: Cornell extension. Keeping: Utah State extension.

tomato.about: Grown for its fruit, which ripens from midsummer until the first frost. Tall types are tied to a cane and kept to one stem by pinching out the side shoots; bush types stay compact and suit pots.
tomato.water: Keep the soil evenly moist: uneven watering splits the fruit and causes blossom end rot. In hot weather a pot can need water every day.
tomato.feed: Once the first fruits swell, give a high-potassium liquid feed (tomato feed) every 10 to 14 days. Rich ground needs less, but a feed every two weeks still raises the crop.
tomato.harvest: Pick each fruit with its stalk once it is fully coloured. At the end of the season, ripen green fruit somewhere warm and dark, or in a drawer with a banana.
tomato.keeps: Ripe fruit keeps a few days at room temperature, out of the sun; the fridge spoils its taste.

problems.name: Blight
problems.fix: Brown patches that spread fast over leaves and fruit in warm, wet weather. Remove affected leaves and fruit as soon as you see them, and grow tomatoes away from potatoes, which share it.

problems.name: Blossom end rot
problems.fix: A dark, sunken patch at the bottom of the fruit, from uneven watering. Water regularly and never let a pot dry out.

problems.name: Split fruit
problems.fix: Cracks in ripening fruit when heavy rain or a big watering follows a dry spell. Keep the soil evenly moist and eat split fruit soon.

tomato.source: Tomato care: RHS. How many to grow: University of Missouri and Kansas State extension. pH: University of Georgia extension. Keeping: University of Arizona extension.

pepper.about: Grown for its sweet fruit, eaten green or left to turn red, yellow or orange. It needs a long, warm summer: in a cool area it does best in a greenhouse or a sunny, sheltered spot. Tie each plant to a cane, as the stems are brittle and snap under a heavy crop.
pepper.water: Keep the soil evenly moist: if it dries out, the flower buds drop. In hot weather a pot can need water every day.
pepper.feed: Once it flowers, give a high-potassium liquid feed (tomato feed) every week to plants in pots. Rich ground needs less, but feeding still raises the crop.
pepper.harvest: Pick when the fruit is full size and glossy, green or once coloured; it gets sweeter as it colours, but fruit left to ripen slows new ones. Cut the stalk with secateurs rather than pulling.
pepper.keeps: Keeps best at cool room temperature; in the fridge, 1 to 3 days if you eat it soon after taking it out.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small green or black insects on shoot tips and under leaves, which curl; the plant stops growing well. Check often and rub or hose off small colonies; ladybirds and other predators help.

problems.name: Blossom end rot
problems.fix: A dark, sunken patch at the bottom of the fruit, from uneven watering. Water regularly; the rest of the crop is usually fine.

problems.name: Flower drop
problems.fix: Buds and flowers fall without setting fruit when the soil dries out, in great heat or on cold nights. Keep the soil evenly moist, and ventilate and shade a greenhouse on hot days.

pepper.source: Pepper care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and Virginia Tech extension. pH: Virginia Tech extension. Keeping: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension.

chilli.about: Grown for hot fruit to use fresh, dried or pickled. It needs warmth all summer: a greenhouse, a sunny windowsill or a warm, sheltered spot outdoors. A plant in a pot can come indoors before the cold and spend the winter in a bright, warm place, watered sparingly.
chilli.water: Keep the compost evenly moist: dry compost makes the buds drop. A pot in full sun can need water every day in hot weather.
chilli.feed: Once it flowers, give a high-potassium liquid feed (tomato feed) every week to plants in pots. Plants in rich ground need less.
chilli.harvest: Pick green for the biggest crop: fruit left to turn red is hotter, but the plant then makes fewer new flowers. Late in the season let the last fruits colour. Cut them with the stalk, and wash your hands after handling hot types.
chilli.keeps: Keep fresh chillies cool and use them soon, or dry, freeze or pickle them for winter.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small green or black insects on shoot tips and under leaves, which curl. Check often, above all indoors, and rub or hose off small colonies; ladybirds and other predators help.

problems.name: Red spider mite
problems.fix: Fine pale mottling on the leaves and thin webbing, in hot, dry air, mostly under cover. Mist the plants and damp down the greenhouse floor to raise the humidity.

problems.name: Few fruits in great heat
problems.fix: Above about 30 °C flowers fall and few fruits set. Ventilate and shade the greenhouse, and damp down the floor every day.

chilli.source: Chilli care and keeping: RHS. pH: Virginia Tech extension (peppers).

aubergine.about: Grown for its glossy fruit, purple, white or striped. It needs more heat than a tomato and about five months from sowing to harvest: in a cool summer grow it in a greenhouse or the sunniest, most sheltered spot. Pinch out the tip at about 30 cm for a bushier plant, and keep five or six fruits on large-fruited types.
aubergine.water: Keep the soil steadily moist; in hot weather a pot can need water every day. Under cover, misting the leaves twice a day also keeps red spider mite away.
aubergine.feed: Once the first flowers open, give a high-potassium liquid feed every two weeks. Rich ground needs less, but feeding still raises the crop.
aubergine.harvest: Cut each fruit with a few centimetres of stalk once it is full size, glossy and well coloured; dull skin means it is over-ripe and may taste bitter. Pick regularly, and mind the small spines on the stalk.
aubergine.keeps: Keeps best at cool room temperature and is eaten within days; in the fridge, 1 to 3 days if you cook it soon after.

problems.name: Few or no fruits
problems.fix: Usually a cool summer or a cold site. Give it the hottest, sunniest spot and steady moisture, and remove flowers that open after late summer: their fruit will not ripen.

problems.name: Red spider mite
problems.fix: Fine pale mottling on the leaves and thin webbing, in hot, dry air under cover. Mist the leaves and damp down the greenhouse floor on hot mornings.

problems.name: Aphids and whitefly
problems.fix: Sap-sucking insects under the leaves, which turn sticky and pale. Check the undersides often and wash off small colonies; in a greenhouse, yellow sticky traps catch whitefly.

aubergine.source: Aubergine care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and Virginia Tech extension. pH: Virginia Tech extension. Keeping: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension.

cucumber.about: Grown for its fruit, picked from midsummer. Most varieties climb: train them up a cane, netting or trellis to save room and keep the fruit clean. Greenhouse types are usually all-female, so remove any male flowers on them; outdoor types need their male flowers for pollination.
cucumber.water: Keep the soil evenly moist, above all once fruit forms. Water at the base in the morning and keep the leaves dry; in a hot spell a pot can need water every day.
cucumber.feed: In the ground it rarely needs feeding unless the soil is poor. In a pot, give a general liquid feed every 10 to 14 days, and switch to a high-potassium feed (tomato feed) once it flowers.
cucumber.harvest: Cut the fruit with a knife at its size: about 15 cm for small types, 20 to 25 cm for full-size ones. Check every few days, as fruit grows fast and regular picking keeps more coming; yellow, swollen fruit is over-ripe.
cucumber.keeps: Keeps best at cool room temperature; in the fridge, 1 to 3 days if you eat it soon after taking it out.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: A white powder on the leaves, worse when the roots are dry. Water at the base, keep the leaves dry and the soil moist, and choose resistant varieties.

problems.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
problems.fix: Yellow mottled, puckered leaves and stunted plants. Pull up and throw away affected plants (not on the compost heap), and keep aphids down, as they spread it.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat young plants, above all in damp weather. Protect plants after planting out and check them at dusk; plants trained upwards keep the fruit out of reach.

cucumber.source: Cucumber care: RHS. How many to grow: Virginia Tech extension. pH: Cornell Cooperative Extension. Keeping: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension.

courgette.about: Grown for its young fruit, picked small all summer; the flowers are good to eat too. One plant spreads wide and crops heavily. Pick often: a fruit left a few days grows into a marrow and slows the plant.
courgette.water: Keep the soil moist all summer, watering the base, not the leaves. A small pot sunk beside each plant and filled with water sends it straight to the roots.
courgette.feed: Dig plenty of compost or well-rotted manure into the soil before planting; in good soil it then needs little more. In a pot, give a high-potassium liquid feed every 10 to 14 days once the first fruits swell.
courgette.harvest: Cut the fruit at 10 to 12 cm long, while small and tender. In good weather check every day or two: one plant can give three or four fruits a week. Male flowers can be picked without losing fruit.
courgette.keeps: Keeps a few days in the fridge; eat it while still firm.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: White powder on the leaves from midsummer, worse in dry soil. Keep the soil moist, water the base, and cut off the worst leaves.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat young plants, flowers and small fruits. Protect plants after planting out, or sow indoors so they go out larger.

problems.name: Fruit rotting or not forming
problems.fix: Small fruits rot from the tip in a cool early summer, when few insects pollinate. It passes as the weather warms; you can also pollinate by hand with a male flower.

courgette.source: Courgette care: RHS. How many to grow: Virginia Tech extension. pH: Virginia Tech extension. Keeping: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension.

pumpkin.about: Grown for big fruit that ripen in autumn and store into winter. The trailing stems need plenty of room. For large fruit keep two or three per plant; for one giant pumpkin, keep only one.
pumpkin.water: Water generously, above all once fruit forms, at the base and not over the leaves. A pot sunk beside the plant and filled with water sends it to the roots.
pumpkin.feed: Dig plenty of compost or well-rotted manure into the planting spot; most plants then need nothing more. For very large fruit, give a high-potassium liquid feed every 10 to 14 days once the fruit swells.
pumpkin.harvest: Leave the fruit to colour fully on the plant; the skin should be hard and not dent under a fingernail. Cut before the first frost with at least 10 cm of stalk, then leave it in the sun for a week to 10 days to harden the skin.
pumpkin.keeps: Store hardened fruit in an airy place at 10 to 15 °C, not touching: at least three months, up to six in good conditions. Frosted fruit does not keep.

problems.name: Fruit rot
problems.fix: Fruit lying on wet soil, or cut with too short a stalk, rots. Set each fruit on a tile, brick or piece of wood, and never carry it by the stalk.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: White powder on the leaves, worse when plants go dry. Water steadily and give plants room for air to move.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat young plants and flowers. Protect plants after planting out, above all in damp weather.

pumpkin.source: Pumpkin care and keeping: RHS. Ripeness: University of Minnesota extension. How many to grow: Kansas State and Virginia Tech extension. pH: Virginia Tech extension.

winter_squash.about: Grown for hard-skinned fruit such as butternut, acorn or onion squash, which store through winter. Trailing types spread far; smaller ones can be trained up a sturdy support. Leave the fruit on the plant until fully ripe: an unripe squash does not keep.
winter_squash.water: Water generously while the fruit swells, at the base and not over the leaves. A mulch around the plants holds moisture in the soil.
winter_squash.feed: Dig plenty of compost or well-rotted manure into the planting spot. On poor soil, give a high-potassium liquid feed every 10 to 14 days once the fruit swells.
winter_squash.harvest: Pick when the skin is hard and dull, does not dent under a fingernail, and the stalk is firm. Cut before the first frost with a long piece of stalk, and leave in the sun for about 10 days to harden.
winter_squash.keeps: Store hardened fruit in a dry, airy place at 10 to 15 °C: one to six months, depending on the type. Check often and use any that soften.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: White powder on the leaves, worse when plants go dry. Water steadily and give plants room for air to move.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat young plants and flowers. Protect plants after planting out, above all in damp weather.

problems.name: Fruit not setting
problems.fix: Small fruits shrivel or rot in cool weather, when few insects pollinate. Pollinate by hand, brushing pollen from a male flower into the female flower, which has a small fruit behind it.

winter_squash.source: Squash care: RHS. Ripeness and keeping: University of Minnesota extension and RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and Virginia Tech extension. pH: Virginia Tech extension.

green_beans.about: Grown for tender pods, picked young. Dwarf types grow to about 45 cm and suit pots; climbing types need tall canes but crop for longer. They die in frost and rot in cold, wet soil, so sow only once the soil is warm.
green_beans.water: Water in dry weather, most of all once the plants flower and set pods; dry soil makes the flowers drop. Pots need water often.
green_beans.feed: Beans need no feed in the ground, and too much nitrogen gives leaves instead of pods. In a pot, give a high-potassium liquid feed every two weeks from the first flowers.
green_beans.harvest: Pick pods at 15 to 20 cm, when they snap cleanly and before the beans show through. Pick every few days: the more you pick, the more pods come.
green_beans.keeps: Pods keep a few days in the fridge in a bag. For winter, blanch and freeze them.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat seedlings overnight. Raise plants in pots and plant them out once sturdy, and check for slugs on damp evenings.

problems.name: Blackfly
problems.fix: Dense black aphids on the shoot tips. Squash them or wash them off with a jet of water.

problems.name: Flowers dropping
problems.fix: Flowers fall without setting pods in hot, dry or windy weather. Keep the soil moist, especially at flowering.

green_beans.source: Bean care: RHS and Virginia Tech extension. How many to grow: Kansas State and Texas A&M extension. pH: Virginia Tech and Penn State extension.

sweetcorn.about: Grown for its sweet cobs. Plant it in a block of short rows rather than one long row: the pollen falls on the wind, and only a block fills the cobs well. Keep supersweet varieties away from other sweetcorn, or the kernels turn starchy.
sweetcorn.water: Water young plants until they are established, then in dry spells, above all when the tassels appear and while the cobs swell.
sweetcorn.feed: Grow it in ground rich in compost or manure. A nitrogen feed when the plants are about knee-high raises the crop.
sweetcorn.harvest: Check the cobs once the silks turn brown: peel back a little husk and press a kernel with a fingernail. Creamy juice means ready, watery means wait; twist the cob off and eat it soon, as its sugar turns to starch.
sweetcorn.keeps: Keep the cobs in the fridge and eat them within 2 days; supersweet types last about a week. Freeze any surplus.

problems.name: Poorly filled cobs
problems.fix: Cobs with gaps where kernels never formed, from poor pollination. Plant in a block, and on a still day tap the tassels to shake the pollen down.

problems.name: Birds and mice
problems.fix: Birds, mice and squirrels eat the seed and the ripening cobs. Sow indoors or net the seed bed, and cover the cobs once they form.

problems.name: Smut
problems.fix: Large grey-white swellings on cobs and stems that burst into black powder. Cut them off before they burst and throw them away, and grow sweetcorn somewhere else next year.

sweetcorn.source: Sweetcorn care: RHS. How many to grow: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension. pH: University of Connecticut and University of Maryland extension. Keeping: University of Missouri extension.

strawberry.about: A perennial grown for its berries: summer-fruiting types crop in early summer, everbearing ones from summer into autumn. A bed crops well for three or four years; then replant in a new spot, using rooted runners, to avoid soil diseases.
strawberry.water: Water regularly in dry spells, and often in pots and hanging baskets, which dry out fast. Water in the morning at the base, keeping the crowns and fruit dry.
strawberry.feed: In ground mulched with compost each spring it rarely needs more. In pots, give a general liquid feed every two weeks, then a high-potassium feed once the flower buds form.
strawberry.harvest: Pick berries when they are red all over, in the warmest part of the day; they do not ripen after picking. Spread straw under the plants as fruits form to keep them clean, and take it away in autumn.
strawberry.keeps: Best eaten the day you pick them; keep them in the fridge and wash them just before eating. Frozen berries lose their shape and suit smoothies and desserts.

problems.name: Grey mould
problems.fix: Fuzzy grey rot on the fruit in wet weather. Water in the morning without splashing, keep fruit on straw, and remove rotten berries straight away.

problems.name: Birds
problems.fix: Birds take the ripening fruit. Cover the plants with taut, well-fixed netting on a frame before the berries colour.

problems.name: Vine weevil
problems.fix: In pots, plants wilt and collapse because white, C-shaped grubs eat the roots. Water a biological control (nematodes) into the compost in late summer.

strawberry.source: Strawberry care: RHS. Pot size: Iowa State University extension. pH: Cornell Cooperative Extension. Keeping: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension.

melon.about: Grown for sweet fruit in late summer. It needs real heat: in a cool area grow it in a greenhouse, tunnel or cold frame. So that the fruits ripen, keep up to four on a plant outdoors and four to six under cover, removing the rest when they are about 2.5 cm across.
melon.water: Keep the soil evenly moist but not soggy, watering in the morning at the base. Water less once the fruit starts to ripen in late summer.
melon.feed: In a pot, give a general liquid feed every 10 to 14 days in early summer, then a high-potassium feed once the fruits are the size of a walnut. Stop feeding as they ripen.
melon.harvest: A ripe melon smells sweet, the stalk starts to crack where it meets the fruit, and the end opposite the stalk gives slightly when pressed. Cantaloupe types then come away from the stalk with a light push.
melon.keeps: A ripe melon keeps a few days at room temperature; once cut, cover it and keep it in the fridge.

problems.name: Fruit not setting
problems.fix: Under cover, few insects reach the flowers. Open vents and doors on warm days, and pollinate by hand with a small brush, from male flowers into female ones, which have a small fruit behind.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: White powder on the leaves, worse when plants go dry. Water steadily and keep the leaves dry.

problems.name: Red spider mite
problems.fix: Fine pale mottling on the leaves and thin webbing, in dry air under cover. Damp down the greenhouse floor and mist the plants in hot weather.

melon.source: Melon care: RHS. Ripeness: University of Minnesota extension. How many to grow: Virginia Tech and Kansas State extension. pH: Virginia Tech extension. Keeping: Kansas State and University of Missouri extension.

watermelon.about: Grown for its large, sweet fruit. It needs a long, hot summer: in a cool area choose a small, early type and grow it under cover. Unlike other melons it does not ripen after picking, so judge ripeness on the plant.
watermelon.water: Water deeply and regularly while the vines grow and the fruit swells, at the base and in the morning. Water less once the fruit is close to full size.
watermelon.feed: Work compost into the soil before planting. Too much nitrogen gives leaves instead of fruit, so if you feed, use a high-potassium feed once fruits form.
watermelon.harvest: It is ripe when the curly tendril nearest the fruit is brown and dry, the patch where it lies on the ground turns from white to creamy yellow, and the skin turns from shiny to dull. Check all three, then cut it with a knife.
watermelon.keeps: A whole watermelon keeps 2 to 3 weeks in a cool place at 10 to 15 °C, away from apples, bananas and tomatoes. Once cut, keep it covered in the fridge.

problems.name: Picked unripe
problems.fix: A watermelon cut too early stays pale and bland, as it does not ripen off the plant. Wait for the dry tendril, yellow ground spot and dull skin together.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: White powder on the leaves, worse when plants go dry. Water steadily at the base and keep the leaves dry.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat young plants. Protect plants after planting out, above all in damp weather.

watermelon.source: Watermelon care: RHS. Ripeness and keeping: University of Minnesota extension. How many to grow: Virginia Tech and Kansas State extension. pH: University of Maryland extension.

basil.about: A tender annual herb grown for its scented leaves, from early summer until the first cold nights. Pinching out the shoot tips keeps the plant bushy and leafy. It grows well in a pot in a warm, sheltered, sunny spot.
basil.water: Keep the soil evenly moist, watering in the morning and at the base rather than over the leaves: basil hates wet roots overnight. Pots in hot weather may need water every day.
basil.feed: In the ground it needs no feeding. In a pot, give a balanced liquid feed every few weeks in summer; avoid tomato feed, which pushes it into flower.
basil.harvest: Pick shoot tips just above a pair of leaves, a few from each plant, so new side shoots grow. Pinch out flower buds as they appear to keep the leaves tender.
basil.keeps: Basil blackens in the fridge: keep the stems in a glass of water at room temperature for a few days. For longer, freeze the chopped leaves in oil or make pesto.

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.fix: Leaves yellow between the veins, with a grey-purple fuzz underneath, mostly in humid weather. Water at the base in the morning, give plants room, and pull out affected plants.

problems.name: Cold damage
problems.fix: Leaves turn black and limp after cold nights. Keep basil indoors until nights stay warm, and bring pots in or cover plants as autumn cools.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They can eat young plants overnight. Grow basil in pots, check after dark and remove them.

basil.source: Basil care: RHS. pH: Clemson and University of Connecticut extension.

parsley.about: A biennial herb grown as an annual for its curly or flat leaves. The seed is slow: it can take up to six weeks to come up outdoors, so mark the row and keep it moist. In its second year it flowers and the leaves lose quality, so sow fresh each year.
parsley.water: Keep the soil moist but not waterlogged, above all while seedlings are small and in hot, dry spells. Pots dry out quickly; move them into light shade in summer heat.
parsley.feed: In the ground it needs no feeding. In a pot, give a balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the growing season.
parsley.harvest: Cut a few outer stems at the base and leave the centre to keep growing; regular picking brings new leaves from late spring to autumn.
parsley.keeps: A bunch keeps several days in the fridge with its stems in water. Chopped leaves freeze well in ice cube trays, and keep more flavour than dried ones.

problems.name: Carrot fly
problems.fix: Larvae tunnel into the roots; plants turn reddish, wilt and stop growing. Cover the bed with fine insect mesh from sowing onwards.

problems.name: Celery leaf miner
problems.fix: Pale brown blisters on the leaves, where larvae feed inside. Pick off and bin the affected leaves; the plant grows new ones.

problems.name: Slow to come up
problems.fix: Nothing shows for weeks, and the row is often dug over by mistake. Soak the seed overnight before sowing, keep the soil moist and wait up to six weeks.

parsley.source: Parsley care: RHS. pH: Cornell and University of Maryland extension.

coriander.about: A fast annual grown for its leaves (cilantro) and later its seeds. It runs to flower quickly in heat and dry soil, so sow small batches every month or so from spring rather than one big sowing. It grows well in a pot.
coriander.water: Keep the soil moist in dry spells: dry roots make it flower early. Check pots every day in warm weather.
coriander.feed: It needs no feeding in garden soil or fresh compost: it is a quick crop.
coriander.harvest: Start cutting leaves when plants are 10 to 15 cm tall, a few from each plant, then let them regrow for about two weeks. For seed, let some plants flower and cut the stems when the seeds turn brown, drying them in a paper bag.
coriander.keeps: A fresh bunch keeps a few days in the fridge. Dried seed keeps for months in an airtight jar.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: Plants send up a flower stalk and stop making leaves, in hot, dry weather or after being transplanted. Sow it where it is to grow, in a spot shaded at midday, water in dry spells and choose a slow-bolting variety.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat the seedlings in damp weather. Check after dark and remove them.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small green or black insects cluster on the shoot tips and weaken the plant. Rub or wash them off and leave ladybirds to feed on them.

coriander.source: Coriander care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut extension. Pot size: Oregon State extension.

dill.about: An annual herb grown for its feathery leaves and its seeds. It has a taproot and dislikes being moved, so sow it where it is to grow, in small batches every few weeks from mid-spring to midsummer. Like coriander, it runs to flower in hot, dry weather.
dill.water: Water in dry spells: dry soil makes it flower early and stop making leaves. Pots dry out quickly in warm weather.
dill.feed: It needs no feeding in garden soil or fresh compost.
dill.harvest: Pick leaves from about six weeks after sowing, a few at a time, leaving at least a third of the plant. For seed, cut the heads in late summer when they are dry and brown and hang them upside down in a paper bag.
dill.keeps: Fresh leaves wilt fast and keep badly, even in the fridge: use them soon, or dry them. Dried leaves and seeds keep in an airtight jar.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: Plants flower early and stop making leaves in hot, dry weather. Water in dry spells, sow every few weeks and cut off flower stems if you only want leaves.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small green or black insects cluster on the soft shoots and leaves. Rub or wash them off and leave ladybirds to feed on them.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat the delicate seedlings in damp weather. Check after dark and remove them.

dill.source: Dill care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut extension.

chervil.about: A small, delicate annual herb with a mild aniseed taste, grown for its leaves. It likes cool weather and light shade and runs to flower in hot sun, so it does best in spring and autumn. Sow small amounts every few weeks for a steady supply.
chervil.water: Keep the soil evenly moist but not waterlogged: dry soil makes it flower early. Pots need extra water in warm weather.
chervil.feed: It needs no feeding in garden soil or fresh compost.
chervil.harvest: Leaves are ready about eight weeks after sowing, once plants are 10 cm tall. Pick a few young leaves from each plant, or cut whole stems back to 5 cm and let them regrow.
chervil.keeps: Chervil is best used fresh: it wilts within a day or two and loses most of its flavour when dried.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: Plants flower early and the leaves lose their taste, in hot sun and dry soil. Grow it in light shade, water regularly and sow again every few weeks.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small green insects cluster on the soft leaves and shoots. Rub or wash them off and leave ladybirds to feed on them.

chervil.source: Chervil care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut extension.

chives.about: A perennial herb grown for its mild onion-flavoured leaves and edible purple flowers. The clump comes back every spring; lift and split it every three or four years to keep it vigorous.
chives.water: Water in dry spells in its first summer; after that, it copes on its own in the ground. In a pot, keep the compost evenly moist.
chives.feed: Needs little: compost at planting is enough in the ground. In a pot, a general liquid feed now and then in summer keeps new leaves coming.
chives.harvest: Snip leaves just above the base whenever you need them; frequent cutting brings more. After flowering, cut the whole clump back to about 5 cm for a flush of fresh leaves.
chives.keeps: Cut chives wilt within a few days. Chop and freeze them, in a bag or ice cube tray, to use in winter.

problems.name: Rust
problems.fix: Orange, raised spots on the leaves. Cut the clump right back and bin the leaves; the new growth is usually clean.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small greenfly clustered on leaves and flower stalks. Rub them off or wash them off with a jet of water.

chives.source: Chive care: RHS. pH: University of Minnesota extension.

thyme.about: A small evergreen shrub grown for its fragrant leaves, picked fresh all year or dried. It needs sun and free-draining soil: wet ground in winter kills it more often than cold does. Plants turn woody after a few years; replace them with new ones from cuttings.
thyme.water: Water new plants in dry spells until they settle; after that, plants in the ground rarely need water. In a pot, water in hot, dry weather and let the compost dry a little in between.
thyme.feed: Thyme grows best in lean soil and needs no feeding in the ground; rich soil gives soft growth with less flavour. A plant in the same pot for over a year can have a light sprinkle of general fertiliser in late spring.
thyme.harvest: Snip sprigs as you need them; the soft new growth of late spring and summer has the best flavour. Regular cutting keeps the plant compact; trim it lightly after flowering, but not into bare wood.
thyme.keeps: Fresh sprigs keep a few days in the fridge in a bag. To dry, hang bunches in a warm, dark, airy place for a few weeks, then keep the leaves in an airtight jar.

problems.name: Root rot
problems.fix: The plant wilts and browns from the base while the soil is wet. Grow it in free-draining soil, a raised bed or a pot with grit, and never leave a pot standing in water.

problems.name: Woody, bare plant
problems.fix: After a few years the centre goes bare and woody. Trim lightly every year after flowering and replace old plants with cuttings taken in late spring.

problems.name: Rosemary beetle
