problems.fix: Small beetles striped metallic green and purple, and their grey larvae, eat the leaves from late summer to spring. Pick them off by hand, or shake the plant over a sheet of paper.

thyme.source: Thyme care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab.

rosemary.about: An evergreen shrub grown for its aromatic leaves, which you can pick all year. It needs full sun and free-draining soil; wet, heavy ground kills it faster than cold. In cold areas grow it against a sunny wall, or in a pot you can move to shelter.
rosemary.water: Water in dry spells during the first year; after that, plants in the ground rarely need water. A pot needs water in hot weather, but never let the compost become waterlogged.
rosemary.feed: Plants in the ground need no feeding. A plant in the same pot for more than a year can have some general granular fertiliser in late spring or early summer.
rosemary.harvest: Snip shoots as you need them all year; the soft new growth of late spring and summer tastes best. Trim after flowering to keep it bushy, but do not cut into old bare wood, which rarely sprouts again.
rosemary.keeps: Fresh sprigs keep several days in the fridge. To dry, hang them in a warm, dark, airy place, then strip the leaves into an airtight jar.

problems.name: Rosemary beetle
problems.fix: Small beetles striped metallic green and purple, and their grey larvae, eat the leaves from late summer to spring. Pick them off by hand, or shake the plant over a sheet of paper.

problems.name: Frost and wet damage
problems.fix: Shoots turn brown and die after a hard frost, cold wind or a wet winter. Cover the plant with fleece in very cold spells, move pots to a sheltered spot, and cut out dead shoots in spring.

problems.name: Cuckoo spit
problems.fix: Blobs of white froth on the shoots in late spring, each hiding a small sap-sucking insect. It does little harm; wipe it off or rinse it away with water.

rosemary.source: Rosemary care: RHS. pH: Texas A&M AgriLife extension.

oregano.about: A spreading perennial grown for its leaves, used fresh or dried. Most of its top growth dies back in winter and new shoots come in spring. It has the most flavour in full sun and lean, free-draining soil, and is best picked just before the flowers open.
oregano.water: Water new plants in dry spells; established plants in the ground need no extra water. In a pot, water in hot, dry weather, but never let the compost stay soggy.
oregano.feed: Plants in the ground need no feeding. A plant in the same pot for more than a year can have a sprinkle of general granular fertiliser in late spring or early summer.
oregano.harvest: Pick shoots from late spring to autumn and strip off the leaves; the flavour is best before the flowers open. Cut it back after flowering for a fresh flush of leaves, and clear the old stems in late winter.
oregano.keeps: Oregano dries well: hang sprigs in a dark, airy place for a few weeks, then strip the leaves into an airtight jar.

problems.name: Mint rust
problems.fix: Orange or brown powdery spots under the leaves, and twisted shoots in spring. Cut affected stems to the ground and put them in the bin, not the compost.

problems.name: Leafhoppers
problems.fix: Pale mottled patches on the leaves from small jumping insects that suck sap. The damage is only cosmetic, so you can leave them.

problems.name: Mint moth
problems.fix: Small caterpillars eat the leaves in summer and spin them together. The damage is usually small; pick off the caterpillars if it bothers you.

oregano.source: Oregano care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab (marjoram) and NC State extension.

sage.about: An evergreen shrub grown for its soft grey-green leaves, which you can pick all year. It needs sun and a soil that never stays waterlogged. Plants turn woody and straggly after six or seven years, so replace them with new ones from cuttings.
sage.water: Water in dry spells during the first year; after that, plants in the ground cope with drought. In a pot keep the compost just moist, not soggy, and in winter move it beside a wall out of the rain.
sage.feed: Plants in the ground need no feeding. A plant in the same pot for more than a year can have a light sprinkle of general granular fertiliser in late spring or early summer.
sage.harvest: Pick young leaves or whole shoots as you need them; spring and summer growth tastes best, and regular picking keeps the plant bushy. Prune it lightly each year in mid to late spring.
sage.keeps: To dry, hang sprigs in a warm, dark, airy place, then keep the leaves in an airtight jar. You can also freeze chopped leaves in an ice cube tray.

problems.name: Rosemary beetle
problems.fix: Small beetles striped metallic green and purple, and their grey larvae, eat the leaves from late summer to spring. Pick them off by hand, or shake the plant over a sheet of paper.

problems.name: Leafhoppers
problems.fix: Pale mottled patches on the leaves from small jumping insects that suck sap. The damage is rarely serious; pick off the worst leaves.

problems.name: Woody, straggly plant
problems.fix: Old plants grow long bare stems with few leaves. Prune lightly every spring, and take softwood cuttings in late spring to replace the plant every few years.

sage.source: Sage care: RHS. pH: UC Master Gardeners, University of California.

mint.about: A vigorous perennial grown for its leaves, for tea, drinks and cooking. Its roots run fast underground and take over a bed, so grow it in a pot, or in a bottomless pot sunk in the ground with the rim above the soil. It dies down in winter and comes back in spring.
mint.water: Keep the soil evenly moist: mint wilts fast in a dry pot. Check pots often in summer and move them into light shade in hot weather.
mint.feed: In the ground it needs little feeding. Give a potted plant liquid fertiliser in spring, then every 4 to 6 weeks while it grows.
mint.harvest: Pick the young shoot tips often from late spring to autumn; regular picking keeps the plant compact and full of fresh growth. Cut flowering stems back to get new leaves.
mint.keeps: Fresh sprigs keep a few days in a glass of water or in the fridge. Freezing keeps the flavour better than drying: freeze leaves in ice cubes.

problems.name: Mint rust
problems.fix: Orange powdery spots under the leaves, and twisted, swollen shoots in spring. Cut affected stems to the ground and bin them; if it comes back every year, start again with healthy plants in a new spot.

problems.name: Spreading everywhere
problems.fix: Runners come up all over the bed. Keep mint in a pot, keep the rim above the soil so runners cannot jump over, and divide and repot every few years.

problems.name: Mint beetle
problems.fix: Small shiny blue-green beetles and their larvae eat holes in the leaves in summer. Pick them off; the plant usually regrows.

mint.source: Mint care: RHS. pH: NSW Department of Primary Industries. Feeding in pots: University of Arizona extension.

tulip.about: Grown for big, bright flowers in mid to late spring. Plant the bulbs late in autumn, which lowers the risk of tulip fire, in free-draining soil that does not stay wet. Many tulips flower well only in their first year, so plant fresh bulbs for the spots that matter most.
tulip.water: Bulbs in the ground need water only after two or three weeks without rain once the shoots are up. Keep pots watered from when the leaves appear, as drought shortens flowering, and move them out of the rain if the compost stays sodden in winter.
tulip.feed: From early spring, give pots a high-potassium liquid feed (tomato feed) every week until the leaves turn yellow.
tulip.harvest: For the vase, cut when the bud shows colour but has not opened. In the garden, cut off faded flowers just above the leaves and leave the leaves until they turn straw-coloured; to keep the bulbs, lift them about six weeks after flowering, dry them and store them somewhere warm, dark and airy until autumn.
tulip.keeps: Cut tulips last several days in a vase and keep growing and bending towards the light; top up with cold water.

problems.name: Tulip fire
problems.fix: Brown spots and twisted, withered leaves and flowers, sometimes with grey mould. Dig out and bin affected plants with their bulbs, plant late in autumn, and grow tulips somewhere else for at least three years.

problems.name: Squirrels and mice
problems.fix: Bulbs dug up and eaten in autumn and winter. Cover the bed or pot with chicken wire until the leaves are up; daffodils planted among them help, as squirrels avoid them.

problems.name: Few or no flowers
problems.fix: Leaves but no flowers, or small flowers, from the second year on. Plant at least three times the bulb's height deep, feed pots while in leaf, and replace tired bulbs with fresh ones.

tulip.source: Tulip care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab. Pot size: Purdue University extension.

daffodil.about: Grown for yellow and white flowers from late winter to mid spring. They come back for many years and slowly spread into clumps, in sun or light shade. The one thing to know: let the leaves die back on their own after flowering, as they feed next year's flowers.
daffodil.water: Bulbs in the ground rarely need water, only in long dry spells while they are in growth. Pots dry out fast: water them until the leaves die down.
daffodil.feed: In the ground they need no feed. In pots, give a high-potassium liquid feed (tomato feed) from when the shoots appear until the leaves start to die down.
daffodil.harvest: Snap off faded flowers so the energy goes back into the bulb. Leave the leaves until they turn yellow, about six weeks after flowering, and do not cut, tie or knot them; for the vase, cut when the bud is about to open.
daffodil.keeps: Cut daffodils ooze a sap that shortens the life of other flowers: stand them in water on their own overnight before mixing them, and do not recut the stems.

problems.name: No flowers (blind daffodils)
problems.fix: Plenty of leaves but no flowers, from crowded clumps, bulbs planted too shallow, or leaves cut off too early. Lift and divide crowded clumps once the leaves have died back, and replant deeper.

problems.name: Narcissus bulb fly
problems.fix: Thin, grassy leaves and no flowers; the bulb is soft, with a fat grub inside. Throw away soft bulbs, and firm the soil over the holes as the leaves die back so the fly cannot reach the bulbs.

problems.name: Basal rot
problems.fix: Bulbs soften and rot from the base, in wet soil or in storage. Plant only firm bulbs in well-drained soil and throw away any that feel soft.

daffodil.source: Daffodil care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab. Pot size: Purdue University extension.

crocus.about: Small corms that flower in late winter and early spring, among the first food of the year for bees. They come back each year and spread into drifts in borders and short grass. Let the leaves die back after flowering, and in a lawn do not mow until they have.
crocus.water: Crocuses in the ground rarely need water. In a pot, keep the compost moist a few centimetres down while the plants are in leaf.
crocus.feed: They need no feeding in the ground. In a pot, a high-potassium liquid feed while in leaf helps next year's flowers.
crocus.harvest: No deadheading is needed. Leave the leaves until they die back; in a lawn, wait to mow until then so the corms build up and spread. Crocuses in pots can be lifted once the leaves have died and kept in paper bags somewhere cool and dry until autumn.

problems.name: Squirrels and mice
problems.fix: Corms dug up and eaten after planting. Cover new plantings with chicken wire or plant under metal mesh until the shoots are up.

problems.name: Birds pecking flowers
problems.fix: Torn, shredded flowers, often yellow ones, pecked by sparrows. Black thread or netting over the clump protects them while they flower.

problems.name: Few flowers
problems.fix: Fewer flowers each year, often because the leaves were mown or cut before they died back, or the spot became too shady. Leave the leaves alone and move clumps to a sunnier spot once they are dormant.

crocus.source: Crocus care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab. Pot size: Purdue University extension.

sunflower.about: Grown for its big summer flowers and for seed that you or the birds can eat. Tall types need a strong cane or a wall to be tied to; dwarf types stay short and suit pots. Protect the seedlings from slugs until they are sturdy.
sunflower.water: Water well in dry spells, at the base of the stem: tall types must not dry out. Plants in pots need water more often, daily in hot weather.
sunflower.feed: Dig compost into the bed before sowing. Once flower buds form, a potassium-rich liquid feed (tomato feed) every two weeks gives bigger flowers.
sunflower.harvest: Cut for the vase in the morning, as the petals start to open. For seed, leave the head on until its back turns brown, cover it with a paper bag or net against birds, then cut it and dry it indoors.
sunflower.keeps: A cut stem lasts about a week in a vase; change the water every couple of days. Dry seed keeps for months somewhere cool, dry and dark.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: Young plants eaten down to the stem overnight. Protect seedlings with a collar or start them in pots and plant out once they are sturdy.

problems.name: Birds
problems.fix: Seeds dug up after sowing, or ripening heads picked clean. Cover new sowings with netting and bag the heads you want to keep.

problems.name: Falling over
problems.fix: Tall stems that lean or snap in wind or after rain. Tie them to a strong cane early, or grow them against a wall or fence.

sunflower.source: Sunflower care: RHS. pH: University of Minnesota extension.

marigold.about: French and African marigolds are grown for bright orange and yellow flowers from early summer until the first frost, in beds, pots and between vegetables. They are easy, but slugs love the young plants. Remove faded flowers and they keep coming.
marigold.water: Water in dry spells, at the base rather than over the flowers. Pots dry out fast in summer and need checking every day.
marigold.feed: Ordinary garden soil is enough; rich soil or too much feed gives leaves instead of flowers. In pots, a liquid feed every few weeks keeps them flowering.
marigold.harvest: Deadhead faded flowers every few days by pinching them off below the head. Cut for the vase when the flowers are fully open.
marigold.keeps: Cut flowers last about a week in a vase; strip the leaves that would sit in the water.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: Holes in leaves and seedlings eaten overnight. Plant out sturdy young plants rather than tiny ones and protect them at night in wet weather.

problems.name: Grey mould
problems.fix: Grey fuzz on flowers and stems in cool, wet weather. Remove the rotting flowers and leave space between plants so they dry quickly.

problems.name: Red spider mite
problems.fix: Pale, speckled leaves and fine webbing in hot, dry weather, mostly in greenhouses and pots. Keep plants watered and mist or hose the undersides of the leaves.

marigold.source: Marigold care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab.

calendula.about: A hardy annual grown for orange and yellow flowers from early summer into autumn; the petals are edible and colour salads and rice. It grows in almost any soil and seeds itself around. Sown in autumn, it overwinters and flowers early the next year.
calendula.water: Once established it copes with dry spells; water seedlings and plants in pots. Keep water off the leaves to slow powdery mildew.
calendula.feed: It needs little: rich soil or a lot of feed gives soft leaves and fewer flowers. Plants in pots can have a liquid feed once a month.
calendula.harvest: Cut flowers for the vase or for petals when fully open, in the morning. Deadhead the rest every few days, or plants turn to seed and stop flowering.
calendula.keeps: Cut flowers last about a week in a vase. Petals dried on paper in a warm, airy place keep for months in a jar.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: A white, dusty coat on the leaves from midsummer, worst in dry soil. Water in dry spells, give plants space and pull out badly affected ones; late sowings stay cleaner.

problems.name: Blackfly
problems.fix: Clusters of small black insects on shoot tips and buds. Rub or spray them off with water; ladybirds and other predators soon follow.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: Seedlings eaten overnight in wet weather. Protect young plants at night until they are well grown.

calendula.source: Calendula care: RHS. pH: Utah State University extension.

nasturtium.about: Grown for bright flowers and peppery leaves, both edible, on plants that trail or climb. It does best in poor, well-drained soil: rich soil gives a mass of leaves and few flowers. Easy from seed, even for children.
nasturtium.water: Water seedlings and plants in pots; in the ground it copes with dry spells once growing. Very dry soil for long stops the flowering.
nasturtium.feed: Do not feed it: feeding gives leaves at the expense of flowers. Grow it in ordinary or poor soil, without compost or manure.
nasturtium.harvest: Pick young leaves and open flowers as you need them, in the morning. Green seeds picked before they harden can be pickled like capers; picking faded flowers keeps new ones coming.
nasturtium.keeps: Leaves and flowers wilt quickly: keep them in a bag in the fridge and use them within a day or two.

problems.name: Blackfly
problems.fix: Dense colonies of black insects under the leaves and on shoot tips. Pick off or hose off the worst shoots; ladybirds and hoverflies soon move in.

problems.name: Cabbage white caterpillars
problems.fix: Green caterpillars that strip leaves in late summer, the same ones that eat cabbages. Check under the leaves and pick them off by hand.

problems.name: All leaves, few flowers
problems.fix: Big lush leaves hiding few flowers, from rich soil or feeding. Stop feeding; next year sow in a poorer, sunny spot.

nasturtium.source: Nasturtium care: RHS and University of Maryland extension.

zinnia.about: A cut flower grown for bold colours from midsummer to the first frost: the more you cut, the more it flowers. It loves heat and sun and sulks in cold, wet weather. It dislikes having its roots disturbed, so sow it where it will flower or in small pots.
zinnia.water: Water deeply in dry spells, at the base: wet leaves bring mildew. Plants in pots need checking every day in summer.
zinnia.feed: Ordinary soil with some compost is enough; too much feed gives soft growth. In pots, a liquid feed every two weeks once flowering starts.
zinnia.harvest: Cut when the flower is fully open and the stem is stiff just below the head (it should not bend when you shake it), cutting low above a pair of leaves. Deadhead the rest so new buds keep coming.
zinnia.keeps: Cut flowers last about a week in a vase; give them fresh water every couple of days.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: A white, dusty coat on the leaves in late summer. Water the soil rather than the leaves, leave space for air and remove the worst leaves; mildew-resistant varieties help.

problems.name: Leaf spots
problems.fix: Brown or dark spots with a pale edge on leaves in wet weather. Remove spotted leaves, water at the base and clear the plants away at the end of the season.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: Seedlings eaten overnight. Protect them at night or raise them in small pots and plant out when sturdy.

zinnia.source: Zinnia care: RHS. pH: University of Florida IFAS extension.

cosmos.about: A tall, airy annual with feathery leaves, grown for daisy flowers from midsummer to the first frost and for cutting. It flowers best in poor to average soil; rich soil gives tall leafy plants with few flowers. Dwarf types suit pots.
cosmos.water: Once established it copes with dry spells; water seedlings, new plants and pots. Too much water, like too much feed, means more leaves than flowers.
cosmos.feed: No feed needed in the ground. Plants in pots can have a high-potassium liquid feed (tomato feed) once a month.
cosmos.harvest: Cut for the vase when the buds are just opening, cutting back to a side shoot. Deadhead faded flowers every few days, or the plant sets seed and stops.
cosmos.keeps: Cut flowers last a few days to a week in a vase; cut them in the cool of the morning.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: Seedlings and young plants eaten overnight. Plant out sturdy plants and protect them at night until they are well grown.

problems.name: All leaves, few flowers
problems.fix: Tall, lush plants that flower late and little, from rich soil, feeding or shade. Stop feeding, keep deadheading; next year use a sunnier, poorer spot.

problems.name: Falling over
problems.fix: Tall plants that flop in wind and rain. Pinch out the tip at about 30 cm for bushier plants and support them with canes or twiggy sticks.

cosmos.source: Cosmos care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab.

sweet_pea.about: A climber grown for scented flowers to cut, from early summer. It needs a support of canes, netting or a fence, and pinching out the tip at about 10 cm gives bushier plants. The one rule: keep picking, because once seed pods form it stops flowering. The pods look like garden peas but are poisonous.
sweet_pea.water: Keep the soil moist all season and water well in dry spells: dry roots cut the flowering short. Pots need water every day in warm weather.
sweet_pea.feed: Dig in plenty of compost or well-rotted manure before sowing or planting. Once growing, a liquid feed every week or two keeps the flowers coming.
sweet_pea.harvest: Cut stems every few days when the lowest flowers on the stem are open, in the morning. Remove any seed pods you find, or the plant stops flowering.
sweet_pea.keeps: Cut stems last a few days in a vase; the more you cut, the more new flowers come.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Green insects on shoot tips and buds; they can spread viruses that streak and twist the plant. Squash or hose them off early; remove plants with streaked, stunted growth.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: A white, dusty coat on the leaves late in summer, worse in dry soil and crowded, still spots. Water in dry spells, keep air moving and cut out affected growth.

problems.name: Bud drop
problems.fix: Flower buds turn yellow and fall before they open, after cold nights or when the roots are dry. Keep the soil moist; it usually stops as the weather settles.

sweet_pea.source: Sweet pea care: RHS. pH: University of Missouri extension. Powdery mildew: Oregon State University extension.

lavender.about: A small evergreen shrub grown for its scented summer flowers, much visited by bees and good for drying. It needs full sun and poor, free-draining soil; chalky soil suits it. The one thing to know: trim it every year after flowering, or it turns leggy and woody.
lavender.water: Water new plants regularly in their first summer; established plants in the ground rarely need water. A pot dries out fast and needs regular water in summer.
lavender.feed: Lavender likes soil low in nutrients and needs no feeding; fertiliser gives soft, floppy growth.
lavender.harvest: Cut stems for drying when the first flowers on the spike open, on a dry morning. In late summer, after flowering, cut off the spent stalks with about 2.5 cm of leafy growth, but never cut into bare wood.
lavender.keeps: Hang small bunches upside down in a dark, airy place until dry; the dried flowers keep their scent for months in a closed jar.

problems.name: Root rot
problems.fix: Plants turn grey and die back in wet, heavy soil, often in winter. Plant on a mound or in a raised bed, add grit to pots, and never leave a pot standing in water.

problems.name: Leggy, woody plant
problems.fix: Bare, woody stems with flowers only at the tips. Trim every year after flowering; an old plant that has gone bare does not regrow from old wood and is best replaced.

problems.name: Rosemary beetle
problems.fix: Small beetles striped metallic green and purple, and their grey larvae, eat the leaves and flowers from late summer to spring. Pick them off by hand, or shake the plant over a sheet of paper.

lavender.source: Lavender care: RHS. pH: University of California IPM and UMass extension.

field_beans.about: A winter green manure: sown in autumn, it covers bare ground through winter, its roots open up heavy soil, and like all beans it adds nitrogen. Dig it in in spring, before the next crop.
field_beans.water: Autumn and winter rain is enough; water only if the soil is dry when you sow.
field_beans.feed: Needs no feed: it makes its own nitrogen, which stays in the soil for the next crop.
field_beans.harvest: In spring, up to flowering, cut the plants down, chop them and let them wilt, then dig them into the top 25 cm of soil. Wait about a month before sowing or planting in that bed.

problems.name: Blackfly
problems.fix: Dense black aphids on the shoot tips in spring. Usually nothing to do, as the plants are dug in soon; if it spreads, cut them down a little earlier.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: The dense cover shelters them, and they move on to the next crop. After digging in, protect young plants and check for slugs on damp evenings.

field_beans.source: Green manure care: RHS. pH: Oregon State University extension.

winter_rye.about: The hardiest green manure: sown from late summer to autumn, it grows through winter, holds the soil, smothers weeds, and its dense roots improve the soil. Dig it in in spring.
winter_rye.water: Rain is enough; water only to get the seed going in a dry autumn.
winter_rye.feed: Needs no feed; it grows even on poor, sandy or acid soil and takes up nitrogen that winter rain would otherwise wash away.
winter_rye.harvest: Cut it down in spring while it is still short and soft, chop it and let it wilt, then dig it into the top 25 cm. Older rye is tough, regrows and holds back the next crop.

problems.name: Holds back small seeds
problems.fix: Rotting rye stops small seeds such as carrots and onions from coming up. Wait about a month after digging in before sowing, or plant out young plants or large seeds such as beans.

problems.name: Cut too late
problems.fix: Left too long, rye grows tall and tough, regrows after cutting and can seed itself. Cut it before it is about 30 cm tall.

winter_rye.source: Rye care: RHS and SARE. pH: University of Vermont extension.

crimson_clover.about: A green manure that adds nitrogen to the soil and covers it with leaves and red flowers that bees visit. Sow from spring to late summer; sown about six to eight weeks before the first frost, it overwinters and grows on in spring.
crimson_clover.water: Keep the seedbed moist until the seedlings are up; after that, rain is usually enough.
crimson_clover.feed: Needs no feed: it makes its own nitrogen and leaves it in the soil.
crimson_clover.harvest: Cut it down when it flowers, before it sets seed; once cut to the ground it does not regrow. Dig it into the top 25 cm or leave it on the surface to rot, and wait about a month before sowing.

problems.name: Self-sown clover
problems.fix: Left to set seed, it comes back as a weed among the next crops. Cut it at flowering.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: The dense leaves shelter them, and they move on to the next crop. After cutting, protect young plants and check for slugs on damp evenings.

crimson_clover.source: Crimson clover care: RHS and SARE. pH: University of California SAREP.

phacelia.about: A fast green manure with feathery leaves and blue flowers that bees love. It covers bare soil, holds on to leftover nutrients and adds organic matter when dug in. It is related to none of the usual vegetables, so it fits anywhere in a rotation.
phacelia.water: Rain is usually enough; water only to get a sowing going in dry soil.
phacelia.feed: Needs no feed: it takes up the nutrients left in the soil and gives them back when it is dug in.
phacelia.harvest: Cut it down when it starts to flower, or just after if you leave it for the bees, but always before it sets seed. Chop it, leave it to wilt for a few days, then dig it into the top of the soil and wait two to three weeks before sowing; an autumn sowing can stay over winter and be dug in in spring.

problems.name: Self-seeding
problems.fix: Seedlings coming up all over the bed after plants were left to seed. Cut it before the flowers go over; pull or hoe the seedlings while small.

problems.name: Skin irritation
problems.fix: The bristly stems and leaves can make some people's skin itch or redden. Wear gloves and long sleeves when you cut and dig it in.

phacelia.source: Phacelia as green manure: RHS. pH: USDA NRCS and British Columbia Ministry of Agriculture.

white_mustard.about: A fast green manure: sown on bare ground, it covers the soil in a few weeks, smothers weeds and adds organic matter when dug in. Sow it from spring to late summer in gaps between crops. It belongs to the cabbage family, so leave it out where clubroot is a problem and count it as a cabbage in your rotation.
white_mustard.water: Rain is usually enough. Water the seed bed only in a dry spell, so the seed comes up evenly.
white_mustard.feed: Needs no feed: it takes up nutrients left in the soil and gives them back when it is dug in.
white_mustard.harvest: Cut it down before it flowers, usually four to eight weeks after sowing; chop the stems, let them wilt for a few days, then dig them into the top layer of soil. Wait two to three weeks before sowing or planting there.

problems.name: Clubroot
problems.fix: As a cabbage relative it can carry clubroot and keep it in the soil. Do not sow it where clubroot has appeared, or just before cabbages, turnips or radishes.

problems.name: Going to seed
problems.fix: In warm weather it flowers within weeks, and its seed comes up as weeds. Check it often in summer and cut it down at the first flowers.

white_mustard.source: Green manure: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut extension.
